title: ADFAC: Automatic detection of facial articulatory features
author: Garg, Hamarneh, et al.
materials: Our proposed method (ADFAC) tackles the current limitations in articulatory measurements by making the measurements free from any sensor placement so that the articulations can occur in natural settings without any discomfort to the speakers. In this paper, recent advancements in computer vision and image processing techniques are leveraged to propose an automatic way to quantify various movements of keypoints on the face. Our method has the advantage that it does not involve any human annotators or placement of any sensors. Furthermore, with the proposed method, different feature types and dimensions such as distance-based, time-based and kinematics-based can be extracted from the articulatory movements recorded in the video. These features are useful in understanding speech articulation and perception.
Computing features from the tracked keypoints.

steps.title: Segment videos into tokens
steps.instruction: Divide each recorded video into separate utterance tokens using the MATLAB implementation of ADFAC.

steps.title: Detect facial keypoints
steps.instruction: Automatically locate facial landmarks on each token: tip of the nose, cupid‑bow of the lips, and the centre point of each eyebrow.

steps.title: Track keypoints over time
steps.instruction: Track the detected keypoints throughout the duration of each token to obtain their frame‑by‑frame trajectories.

steps.title: Compute articulatory features
steps.instruction: From the tracked trajectories calculate distance‑based, time‑based and kinematics‑based features for each token.

steps.title: Classify with random forest
steps.instruction: Apply a variant of random‑forest classification to the extracted features, obtaining both feature‑importance scores and statistical significance for each feature.

steps.title: Manual annotation for validation
steps.instruction: Validate detection and tracking accuracy by manual annotation:

substeps.instruction: A volunteer (not involved in the study) uses MATLAB’s ginput.m to trace the left eyebrow, nose and lip curves on the first frame of one randomly sampled token from each of 14 subjects (9 females, 5 males).

For tracking validation, extract frames #4, #8, #16, #64 and #128 from two randomly sampled video tokens (one male, one female) and have the same volunteer annotate the same three facial regions on each frame.

steps.title: Calculate error metrics
steps.instruction: Quantify the discrepancy between automatic and manual landmarks:

substeps.instruction: Compute the Euclidean distance (in pixels) between each automatically detected point of interest (POI) and the nearest manually traced point.
Convert pixel errors to percentages using the video resolution of 1080 × 1920 pixels.
